options.a: Fibrous tissue binding bones with little or no movement
options.b: A fibrocartilage pad joining bones, as in the pubic symphysis
options.c: A joint cavity with synovial fluid and articular cartilage
options.d: Hyaline cartilage plates joining bones, as in growth plates

distractorExplanations.a: Bones bound by fibrous tissue with little movement describe fibrous joints (synarthroses such as sutures), not synovial joints.
distractorExplanations.b: A fibrocartilage pad like the pubic symphysis is a cartilaginous joint (amphiarthrosis) with no synovial cavity.
distractorExplanations.d: Hyaline cartilage plates such as epiphyseal plates are synchondroses, cartilaginous joints without a capsule or cavity.

options.a: Stratified squamous epithelium with keratinized surface cells
options.b: Dense irregular connective tissue with collagen and elastin
options.c: Adipose tissue and loose areolar connective tissue
options.d: Dense regular connective tissue in parallel collagen bundles

distractorExplanations.a: Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium is the epidermis, the layer above the dermis.
distractorExplanations.c: Adipose and loose areolar tissue make up the hypodermis (subcutaneous layer) below the dermis.
distractorExplanations.d: Parallel collagen bundles are dense regular tissue found in tendons and ligaments; dermal collagen runs in irregular directions.

options.a: Pancreatic alpha cells
options.b: Adrenal cortex cells
options.c: Pancreatic beta cells
options.d: Thyroid C cells

distractorExplanations.a: Pancreatic alpha cells secrete glucagon, which raises blood glucose; insulin comes from beta cells.
distractorExplanations.b: The adrenal cortex secretes cortisol, aldosterone, and androgens, not insulin.
distractorExplanations.d: C cells: calcitonin.

options.a: A sensory neuron and the muscle spindle it monitors
options.b: A single muscle fiber and all the motor neurons supplying it
options.c: A bundle of muscle fibers wrapped in perimysium
options.d: A motor neuron and the muscle fibers it innervates

distractorExplanations.a: A sensory neuron with its muscle spindle is an afferent receptor unit; a motor unit is an efferent neuron plus its fibers.
distractorExplanations.b: This reverses the structure: one motor neuron supplies many fibers, and each fiber is normally supplied by one neuron.
distractorExplanations.c: A bundle of fibers wrapped in perimysium is a fascicle, a connective tissue grouping, not a motor unit.

options.a: Return interstitial fluid to the bloodstream and support immune function
options.b: Carry oxygenated blood from the heart to capillary beds
options.c: Carry deoxygenated blood from tissues back to the right atrium
options.d: Absorb amino acids and glucose from the gut into the hepatic portal vein

distractorExplanations.b: Carrying oxygenated blood to capillary beds is the job of arteries and arterioles, not lymphatic vessels.
distractorExplanations.c: Returning deoxygenated blood to the right atrium is the venous system; lymphatics return interstitial fluid, not blood.
distractorExplanations.d: Lacteals absorb dietary fats; amino acids and glucose enter blood capillaries that drain to the hepatic portal vein.

options.a: Amplification of a change until a process is complete
options.b: Maintenance of a relatively stable internal environment
options.c: Breakdown of complex molecules to release cellular energy
options.d: Sum of all chemical reactions occurring in the body's cells

distractorExplanations.a: Amplifying a change until an endpoint (as in childbirth) is positive feedback, not the stable state homeostasis maintains.
distractorExplanations.c: Breaking down molecules to release energy is catabolism, one part of metabolism, not homeostasis.
distractorExplanations.d: The sum of all chemical reactions in the body is metabolism, not the maintenance of a stable internal environment.

options.a: Triceps brachii (with anconeus)
options.b: Biceps brachii (with brachialis)
options.c: Coracobrachialis (with deltoid)
options.d: Pronator teres (with supinator)

distractorExplanations.a: Triceps brachii and anconeus are the elbow extensors, the antagonists of elbow flexion.
distractorExplanations.c: Coracobrachialis and the anterior deltoid flex the shoulder, not the elbow.
distractorExplanations.d: Pronator teres and supinator rotate the forearm; pronator teres is at most a weak assistant in elbow flexion.

options.a: Dense fibrous tissue that tightly binds bones with no cavity
options.b: A fluid-filled joint cavity allowing relatively free movement
options.c: A fibrocartilage disc linking bones with slight movement
options.d: Hyaline cartilage joining two bones that later ossifies with age

distractorExplanations.a: Bones bound by dense fibrous tissue without a cavity are fibrous joints such as sutures, not synovial joints.
distractorExplanations.c: A fibrocartilage disc allowing slight movement is a symphysis, a cartilaginous amphiarthrosis without a synovial cavity.
distractorExplanations.d: Hyaline cartilage that ossifies with age describes a synchondrosis such as a growth plate, not a synovial joint.

options.a: Prime mover primarily responsible for a given action
options.b: Muscle that opposes the action and lengthens as it occurs
options.c: Muscle that assists the prime mover in producing the action
options.d: Muscle that fixes a proximal bone so the action can occur

distractorExplanations.b: A muscle that opposes the action and lengthens during it is the antagonist, not the agonist.
distractorExplanations.c: A muscle that assists the prime mover is a synergist; the agonist is the prime mover itself.
distractorExplanations.d: A muscle that fixes a proximal bone is a stabilizer (fixator), not the prime mover of the action.

options.a: Muscle shortens as tension overcomes the load
options.b: Muscle tension increases without changing muscle length
options.c: Muscle lengthens while producing tension under an external load
options.d: Muscle contracts at a constant speed through the range

distractorExplanations.a: Shortening as tension overcomes the load is a concentric contraction, not isometric.
distractorExplanations.c: Lengthening while producing tension under load is an eccentric contraction, not isometric.
distractorExplanations.d: Contraction at a constant speed through the range is isokinetic, usually on a machine, not isometric.

options.a: An exaggerated lateral curvature of the thoracic or lumbar spinal column
options.b: An exaggerated posterior curvature of the thoracic spine
options.c: A loss of the normal anterior curve in the lumbar spine
options.d: An exaggerated anterior curvature of the lumbar (or cervical) spine

distractorExplanations.a: A lateral curvature of the thoracic or lumbar spine is scoliosis, not lordosis.
distractorExplanations.b: An exaggerated posterior thoracic curve is kyphosis, the opposite direction to lordosis.
distractorExplanations.c: Losing the normal lumbar curve is flat back (hypolordosis), the opposite of an exaggerated lordosis.

options.a: Median nerve at the wrist
options.b: Ulnar nerve at the wrist
options.c: Radial nerve at the elbow
options.d: Median nerve at the elbow

distractorExplanations.b: Ulnar nerve compression at the wrist occurs in Guyon's canal, affecting the ring and little fingers, not carpal tunnel.
distractorExplanations.c: Radial nerve compression near the elbow is radial tunnel syndrome, not carpal tunnel syndrome.
distractorExplanations.d: Median nerve compression near the elbow is pronator teres syndrome; carpal tunnel compresses it at the wrist.

options.a: Degeneration of a tendon, whereas tendinosis is inflammatory
options.b: Inflammation of a tendon sheath, whereas tendinosis is a tear
options.c: Inflammation of a tendon, whereas tendinosis is degenerative
options.d: Inflammation of a bursa, whereas tendinosis is degenerative

distractorExplanations.a: This reverses the terms: tendinitis implies inflammation and tendinosis implies degeneration without inflammation.
distractorExplanations.b: Inflammation of the tendon sheath is tenosynovitis, and tendinosis is degeneration, not a tear.
distractorExplanations.d: Inflammation of a bursa is bursitis; tendinitis refers to the tendon itself.

mblex-readiness-check-kinesiology-007.explanation: Modern language often uses tendinopathy; exam content may distinguish inflammatory vs degenerative tendon pathology. Tendinitis is the acute inflammatory concept.

options.a: Patellofemoral pain syndrome around the anterior kneecap
options.b: Pes anserine bursitis at the medial proximal tibia
options.c: Patellar tendinopathy at the inferior pole of the kneecap in jumpers
options.d: IT band friction syndrome near the lateral femoral epicondyle

distractorExplanations.a: Patellofemoral pain is felt around the front of the kneecap, not at the lateral femoral epicondyle under the IT band.
distractorExplanations.b: Pes anserine bursitis causes medial knee pain at the proximal tibia, not lateral IT band pain.
distractorExplanations.c: Patellar tendinopathy (jumper's knee) causes anterior pain below the kneecap, not lateral knee pain.

options.a: Detection of pain from tissue damage
options.b: Sense of body position and movement
options.c: Detection of skin temperature changes
options.d: Detection of blood pressure changes

distractorExplanations.a: Detecting pain from tissue damage is the role of nociceptors, not proprioceptors.
distractorExplanations.c: Detecting temperature changes in the skin is the role of thermoreceptors, not proprioceptors.
distractorExplanations.d: Detecting blood pressure changes is the role of baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch.

options.a: Muscle shortens while lifting a constant load
options.b: Muscle develops tension without changing length
options.c: Muscle lengthens while controlling a load
options.d: Muscle moves at a constant set speed

distractorExplanations.a: Shortening while lifting a load is a concentric (isotonic) contraction, not isometric.
distractorExplanations.c: Lengthening while controlling a load is an eccentric contraction, not isometric.
distractorExplanations.d: Movement at a constant set speed is isokinetic, usually on a dynamometer, not isometric.

options.a: Opposes the desired movement and relaxes
options.b: Primarily produces a desired movement
options.c: Assists the main muscle in the movement
options.d: Steadies a bone so movement can occur

distractorExplanations.a: The muscle that opposes the movement and relaxes is the antagonist, not the prime mover.
distractorExplanations.c: A muscle that assists the main mover is a synergist, not the agonist itself.
distractorExplanations.d: A muscle that steadies a bone is a fixator (stabilizer), not the prime mover.

options.a: The distal segment moving freely in space (e.g., leg extension)
options.b: The distal segment fixed against a surface (e.g., squat)
options.c: Muscle length staying constant against a fixed resistance
options.d: Constant-speed movement on a dynamometer (e.g., isokinetic knee test)

distractorExplanations.a: A distal segment moving freely in space, as in a seated leg extension, is open-chain exercise.
distractorExplanations.c: Constant muscle length describes an isometric contraction type, not the closed kinetic chain classification.
distractorExplanations.d: Constant-speed dynamometer work is isokinetic exercise, defined by speed, and a seated knee test is open chain.

options.a: An excessive posterior curvature of the thoracic (upper back) spine
options.b: An excessive anterior curvature of the lumbar (or cervical) spine
options.c: A lateral curvature of the spine combined with vertebral rotation
options.d: A forward slippage of one vertebra over the one below

distractorExplanations.a: An excessive posterior thoracic curve is kyphosis, not lordosis.
distractorExplanations.c: A lateral curve with vertebral rotation is scoliosis, not lordosis.
distractorExplanations.d: Forward slippage of a vertebra is spondylolisthesis, a structural defect rather than a curvature.

options.a: Nature of treatment, benefits/risks, alternatives, and voluntary agreement
options.b: Nature of treatment and a signed waiver releasing the therapist from liability
options.c: A one-time signature at intake that covers all future sessions
options.d: The therapist's diagnosis and the expected cure for the condition

distractorExplanations.b: A liability waiver is not informed consent; consent requires understanding risks, benefits, and alternatives and stays revocable.
distractorExplanations.c: Consent is ongoing; the client can modify or withdraw it at any time, so one intake signature is not enough.
distractorExplanations.d: Massage therapists do not diagnose or promise cures; consent covers treatment nature, benefits, risks, and alternatives.

options.a: Treatment of the entire body must be avoided until the condition resolves
options.b: Treatment may proceed with modification/caution or physician clearance
options.c: Only the affected area must be avoided while the rest is treated
options.d: Treatment may proceed normally once the client signs a consent form

distractorExplanations.a: Avoiding treatment of the whole body is an absolute (systemic) contraindication, not a relative one.
distractorExplanations.c: Avoiding just the affected area is a local contraindication; relative means treatment can proceed with modification.
distractorExplanations.d: A consent form does not remove the need to modify technique or get clearance for a relative contraindication.

mblex-readiness-check-assessment-treatme.explanation: Absolute contraindications prohibit treatment; relative require adaptation. Whether to adapt depends on how the condition presents.

options.a: Activities (client's daily tasks and goals)
options.b: Allergies (client's reported sensitivities)
options.c: Assessment (therapist's clinical impression)
options.d: Advice (home care given to the client)

distractorExplanations.a: Client-reported activities and goals belong in the Subjective section; A stands for Assessment.
distractorExplanations.b: Allergies are client-reported health history recorded in the Subjective section, not the Assessment.
distractorExplanations.d: Home care and self-care advice is recorded in the Plan section; A stands for Assessment.

options.a: Trigger points refer pain to distant areas when compressed
options.b: Muscles are the most hypertonic and so need the deepest sustained pressure
options.c: Bony landmarks are palpated to locate and confirm muscle attachments
options.d: Underlying structures warrant caution or avoidance of deep pressure

distractorExplanations.a: Referral of pain on compression describes trigger points, not endangerment sites over vulnerable structures.
distractorExplanations.b: This reverses the concept: endangerment sites call for lighter pressure because nerves, vessels, or organs lie close.
distractorExplanations.c: Palpating bony landmarks to find attachments is palpation technique, not the definition of an endangerment site.

mblex-readiness-check-assessment-treatme.explanation: Examples include anterior neck, axilla, abdomen—use caution appropriate to training/laws. Those underlying structures include nerves, vessels, and viscera.

options.a: Gliding strokes used to apply lubricant and warm tissue
options.b: Kneading strokes that lift and squeeze the muscle tissue
options.c: Rhythmic percussive strokes such as hacking and cupping
options.d: Small circular strokes applied across the fiber direction

distractorExplanations.b: Lifting and squeezing tissue is petrissage (kneading), not effleurage.
distractorExplanations.c: Hacking and cupping are percussive tapotement strokes, not gliding effleurage.
distractorExplanations.d: Small strokes across the fiber direction are friction techniques, not long gliding effleurage.

options.a: Increase lymph flow through light rhythmic strokes directed toward the nodes
options.b: Mobilize scar tissue/adhesions in tendons or ligaments with caution
options.c: Sedate the nervous system through slow broad gliding strokes
options.d: Release trigger points with sustained ischemic compression

distractorExplanations.a: Light rhythmic strokes to move lymph describe manual lymphatic drainage, not deep transverse friction.
distractorExplanations.c: Slow broad gliding strokes for relaxation are effleurage; transverse friction is specific and cross-fiber.
distractorExplanations.d: Sustained ischemic compression is trigger point therapy, not cross-fiber friction on scar tissue or adhesions.

options.a: Proceed with light Swedish massage and suggest a doctor visit if pain persists
options.b: Treat the painful area with deep tissue to reduce night pain and then reassess
options.c: Refer to a physician; do not treat as simple musculoskeletal without clearance
options.d: Document the symptoms and continue treatment until the next scheduled session

distractorExplanations.a: Red flags such as night pain with weight loss call for referral before treatment, not a wait-and-see approach.
distractorExplanations.b: Deep work over unexplained night pain can mask or worsen serious pathology; medical clearance comes first.
distractorExplanations.d: Documenting red flags is required, but continuing treatment without referral delays needed medical evaluation.

mblex-readiness-check-assessment-treatme.explanation: Red flags warrant medical referral rather than aggressive massage assumptions. Unexplained weight loss and night pain are red flags.

options.a: Use light effleurage toward the heart to reduce the calf swelling
options.b: Massage only distal to the swelling and elevate the limb
options.c: Apply moist heat and gentle stretching to ease the calf cramping and discomfort
options.d: Avoid massage to the affected limb and seek urgent medical evaluation

distractorExplanations.a: Even light strokes on a limb with suspected DVT can dislodge the clot and cause a pulmonary embolism.
distractorExplanations.b: Massage anywhere on the affected limb risks moving the clot; the limb is avoided and the client referred urgently.
distractorExplanations.c: Heat and stretching over a suspected DVT are unsafe and delay the urgent medical evaluation required.

options.a: Alignment of landmarks from multiple views for asymmetries
options.b: Active and passive range of motion measured at each major joint
options.c: Muscle strength graded against manual resistance
options.d: Gait pattern while the client walks across the room

distractorExplanations.b: Active and passive range of motion testing is a separate assessment, not static postural observation.
distractorExplanations.c: Grading strength against resistance is manual muscle testing, not postural assessment.
distractorExplanations.d: Watching the client walk is gait analysis, a dynamic assessment rather than static posture observation.

options.a: The client has chronic muscle tightness without any injury
options.b: Acute inflammation, instability, or client pain responses
options.c: The tissue has been warmed with effleurage beforehand
options.d: The client has reduced range of motion from inactivity

distractorExplanations.a: Chronic tightness without injury is an indication for stretching, not a reason to avoid it.
distractorExplanations.c: Warming tissue first is recommended preparation for stretching, not a reason to avoid or modify it.
distractorExplanations.d: Stiffness from disuse is a common reason to stretch; it does not signal acute tissue damage.

mblex-readiness-check-assessment-treatme.explanation: Respect pain, healing stages, and joint stability; ballistic stretching can be risky. These signs indicate that the tissue needs protection.

options.a: Rhythmic percussive strokes such as hacking and tapping
options.b: Gliding strokes used to warm tissue and spread lubricant
options.c: Kneading strokes that lift, squeeze, and release tissue
options.d: Fine trembling or shaking movements applied to the tissue

distractorExplanations.a: Hacking and tapping are percussive tapotement strokes, not gliding effleurage.
distractorExplanations.c: Lifting, squeezing, and releasing tissue is petrissage, not effleurage.
distractorExplanations.d: Fine trembling or shaking movements are vibration, a separate Swedish stroke category.

options.a: Trigger points refer pain to distant areas
options.b: Nerves, vessels, or organs are vulnerable
options.c: Muscles attach to bony landmarks
options.d: Lymph nodes require deep sustained pressure

distractorExplanations.a: Pain referral on compression describes trigger points, not endangerment sites over vulnerable structures.
distractorExplanations.c: Muscle attachments at bony landmarks are palpation reference points, not the definition of endangerment sites.
distractorExplanations.d: Lymph nodes are themselves vulnerable structures at endangerment sites and call for light pressure, not deep.

mblex-readiness-check-assessment-treatme.explanation: Endangerment sites require caution due to superficial vessels, nerves, or organs. Deep pressure over these sites should be avoided or modified.

options.a: Client-reported pain levels, history, and session goals
options.b: Objective findings such as posture, ROM, and palpation results
options.c: Therapist's interpretation of the client's progress and treatment response
options.d: Home care advice and the schedule for future sessions

distractorExplanations.a: Client-reported pain, history, and goals belong in the Subjective section, not Objective.
distractorExplanations.c: The therapist's interpretation of progress and response belongs in the Assessment section.
distractorExplanations.d: Home care advice and future session scheduling belong in the Plan section.

options.a: Continue with deep cervical work to release the compressed nerve root
options.b: Stop or modify treatment and refer for appropriate medical evaluation
options.c: Apply traction and strong stretching to decompress the cervical spine
options.d: Finish the session as planned and recommend rest if symptoms continue

distractorExplanations.a: Deep cervical pressure can aggravate nerve root compression; radiating neurologic signs call for referral.
distractorExplanations.c: Forceful traction and stretching of a compromised cervical spine are risky and beyond the massage scope.
distractorExplanations.d: Finishing as planned ignores neurologic red flags and delays the medical evaluation the client needs.

mblex-readiness-check-assessment-treatme.explanation: Red-flag neurologic symptoms warrant caution, modification, and referral as appropriate. Radiating neurologic pain with compression signs is a red flag.

options.a: Protect private health information and disclose only with consent or legal requirement
options.b: Release records to a client's adult family member who asks on the client's behalf
options.c: Discuss client health details with referring friends who booked the session
options.d: Keep information private during treatment but share it freely after the client is discharged

distractorExplanations.b: Family members need the client's written authorization; asking on the client's behalf does not permit disclosure.
distractorExplanations.c: The person who referred or booked the client has no right to health details without the client's consent.
distractorExplanations.d: The duty of confidentiality continues after the therapeutic relationship ends.

options.a: Involve any contact with a client outside the treatment room
options.b: Impair professional judgment or risk exploitation of the client
options.c: Involve accepting a client's referral of a friend or family member
options.d: Continue after the client signs a consent form approving them

distractorExplanations.a: Incidental contact outside the session is not unethical in itself; the test is impaired judgment or exploitation.
distractorExplanations.c: Accepting referrals is normal practice and does not by itself create an unethical dual relationship.
distractorExplanations.d: A signed consent form does not decide the issue; the relationship is unethical if it impairs judgment or risks exploitation.

options.a: Only intercourse; sexual comments are a matter of taste
options.b: Sexual contact during sessions but not after termination
options.c: Any sexualized behavior or contact with a client
options.d: Unintentional draping slips the therapist promptly corrects

distractorExplanations.a: Sexual comments, jokes, and gestures are sexual misconduct too; it is not limited to intercourse.
distractorExplanations.b: Codes and many state laws also bar sexual relationships with clients for a period after the professional relationship ends.
distractorExplanations.d: An accidental draping slip that is promptly corrected is a draping error to document, not sexual misconduct.

mblex-readiness-check-ethics-business-00.explanation: Zero tolerance: sexual activity with clients violates ethics/law; draping and professionalism protect safety. It is prohibited in every circumstance.

options.a: Perform any technique learned in continuing education courses
options.b: Perform services allowed in the state where they completed their training
options.c: Perform any technique the client requests and consents to
options.d: Perform only techniques/services allowed by education and state law

distractorExplanations.a: Continuing education training does not expand the legal scope set by the state practice act.
distractorExplanations.b: Scope of practice is set by the law of the state where the therapist practices, not where they trained.
distractorExplanations.c: Client consent cannot expand scope; techniques outside education and state law stay prohibited.

options.a: Proving clinical outcomes to insurers so higher session fees are justified
options.b: Taxes, legal compliance, and transparent client business relationships
options.c: Replacing SOAP notes as the legal record of each treatment session provided
options.d: Sharing client payment data with marketing partners

distractorExplanations.a: Financial records document transactions; they do not prove clinical outcomes or justify fees.
distractorExplanations.c: Receipts do not replace SOAP notes; clinical documentation is a separate record of treatment.
distractorExplanations.d: Sharing client payment data with marketers breaches privacy; it is not a purpose of accurate recordkeeping.

options.a: The client holds greater power because they pay for and direct the session
options.b: Power is equal once the client signs informed consent for treatment
options.c: The imbalance ends once a client has had several sessions with the therapist
options.d: The therapist holds greater power/influence and must not exploit the client

distractorExplanations.a: Paying for the session does not offset the client's vulnerability; the therapist holds the greater power.
distractorExplanations.b: Informed consent does not equalize power; the imbalance from the therapist's role and the client's vulnerability remains.
distractorExplanations.c: The power differential persists for the whole therapeutic relationship, not just the first sessions.

options.a: Selling expensive unnecessary supplements for personal profit
options.b: Referring a client to a physician for red-flag symptoms
options.c: Charging a published, consistent fee for every client
options.d: Recommending a stretch the client can do at home for free

distractorExplanations.b: Referring red-flag symptoms to a physician is an ethical duty serving the client, not a conflict of interest.
distractorExplanations.c: A published, consistent fee is transparent business practice and creates no conflict of interest.
distractorExplanations.d: Free home stretches bring the therapist no personal gain, so they do not create a conflict of interest.

mblex-readiness-check-ethics-business-00.explanation: Exploitation for financial gain violates ethics; referrals and hygiene are proper. Pressure tactics make the exploitation worse.

options.a: A client's disclosed past drug use with no current risk
options.b: Suspected child/elder abuse according to state statutes
options.c: A client's HIV status shared during the intake interview
options.d: A coworker's lateness to scheduled client appointments

distractorExplanations.a: Past drug use with no current risk is confidential health information, not a mandated report.
distractorExplanations.c: HIV status shared at intake is confidential; massage therapists are not mandated reporters of it.
distractorExplanations.d: A coworker's lateness is an employment matter, not a statutory mandatory reporting duty.

options.a: A signed liability waiver that cannot be revoked once treatment begins
options.b: Explanation of the plan, risks/benefits, and client agreement before treatment
options.c: Explanation of the plan after treatment so the client is not anxious
options.d: Verbal agreement from the person who booked the appointment for the client

distractorExplanations.a: Consent can be withdrawn at any time; an irrevocable liability waiver is not informed consent.
distractorExplanations.c: Consent must be obtained before treatment; explaining the plan afterward means the client never agreed to it.
distractorExplanations.d: Consent comes from the client (or a legal guardian), not from whoever booked the appointment.

mblex-readiness-check-ethics-business-01.explanation: Clients must understand and agree to the nature of treatment and boundaries. Risks and benefits are explained as relevant to the session.

options.a: Increase the client's trust in the therapist and treatment compliance
options.b: Can create conflicts of interest and boundary violations
options.c: Violate state law in every case where they occur
options.d: Reduce the therapist's income from repeat clients

distractorExplanations.a: Overlapping relationships tend to blur boundaries and compromise objectivity rather than build appropriate trust.
distractorExplanations.c: Most dual relationships are ethical rather than legal issues; the concern is conflict of interest and boundaries.
distractorExplanations.d: Income effects are not the ethical concern; the risk is conflicts of interest and boundary violations.

options.a: Share client details with family members who call to ask about the client's progress
options.b: Protect health information and disclose only with authorization or legal requirement
options.c: Discuss clients by name with coworkers who are not involved in their care
options.d: Post before-and-after photos online with faces blurred but no client consent

distractorExplanations.a: Family members need the client's authorization before any health information is shared with them.
distractorExplanations.c: Coworkers not involved in a client's care have no need to know, so naming clients to them breaches confidentiality.
distractorExplanations.d: Client photos still need written consent before use; blurring faces does not replace authorization.

options.a: Assessing posture and range of motion before treatment
options.b: Diagnosing medical conditions or prescribing drugs
options.c: Recommending self-care stretches within their training
options.d: Obtaining a health history and referring red flags

distractorExplanations.a: Postural and range of motion assessment is within massage scope; diagnosis of disease is what is excluded.
distractorExplanations.c: Self-care stretch recommendations within training are generally within massage scope in US practice acts.
distractorExplanations.d: Taking a health history and referring red flags are core in-scope duties, not exclusions.

options.a: The client holds more authority because they pay for the session
options.b: The therapist holds professional authority and must not exploit the client
options.c: The imbalance disappears once the client and therapist become friends
options.d: Both parties hold equal authority once informed consent is signed

distractorExplanations.a: Paying for the session does not give the client more power; the therapist's role and the client's vulnerability do the opposite.
distractorExplanations.c: Friendship creates a dual relationship and does not erase the power differential.
distractorExplanations.d: Informed consent does not equalize power; the therapist keeps professional authority throughout.

mblex-readiness-check-ethics-business-01.explanation: Therapists must manage the inherent power imbalance ethically and non-exploitatively. Clients are vulnerable when unclothed and in pain.
